newsitem.title: USA: New York area community banks see opportunties.
newsitem.headline: New York area community banks see opportunties.

text.p: Top executives from five community banks and thrift institutions headquartered in New York and New Jersey told Wall Street analysts their companies have thrived in the midst of a bank consolidation wave by sharpening their business focus and being more nimble than larger rivals.

"This has been a wonderful opportunity for us," said Gerard Keegan, chairman president and chief executive of Greater New York Savings Bank, a $2.6 billion asset thrift. Most of the thrift's 14 branches are located in Brooklyn, where the thrift was founded in 1897.

Keegan said urban consumers become unhappy when a merger results in branch closings and they have to walk six blocks to their bank instead of three blocks. In the thrift's quarterly earnings on Thursday, third-quarter pre-tax net income rose 88 percent to $8.3 million from $4.4 million a year ago.

Robert Berger, chief financial officer of Syracuse, N.Y.-based ONBANCorp Inc, a $5.36 billion asset commercial bank, said earnings per share for the first nine months of 1996, excluding a charge for the Savings Association Insurance Fund (SAIF), were up 17 percent from a year ago. Operating earnings in the latest quarter were $0.84 per share.

After the formal presentation to the New York Society of Security Analysts, ONBANCorp chief executive Robert Bennett told a reporter he was "easily comfortable" with Wall Street estimates that the bank will earn $3.05 per share this year and $3.33 per share in 1997.

He also said while the company, which has transformed itself from a thrift into a commercial bank, is intent on developing its business, it will act in the best interest of shareholders if it receives a takeover offer at a big premium.
Separately, ONBANCorp said Friday it has sued a Florida shareholder who has been pressing for a sale of the bank.
The suit alleges the shareholder has disseminated false and misleading information about ONBANCorp.

Leonard Simon, chairman, president and chief executive of Rochester, N.Y.-based thrift holding company RCSB Financial Inc, said the company has retreated from problem areas such as commercial real estate and built up niche areas like auto lending. At the end of August, auto loans, with a very low credit loss rate, were 46.6 percent of the total $2 billion in loans. The company's American Credit Services Inc auto lending unit is active in New York state and Florida and seeking to expand into the mid-Atlantic area, Simon said.

"We expect to continue to be an active participant" in industry consolidation, Kenneth Neilson, president and chief executive of HUBCO Inc, a $2.72-billion asset commercial bank headquartered in Mahwah, N.J., told the meeting. He noted that while the company has made 15 acquisitions since the fall of 1990, it has not done any in the past year in its home state of New Jersey but has been active in Connecticut.
Neilson said with valuations on banking companies higher than in the past, a new industry trend seems to be acquisitions of distinct lines of business.

Anthony Abbate, chief executive of Interchange Financial Services Corp, a $493 million-asset commercial bank based in Saddle Brook, N.J., said one of the company's strong points is its base in Bergen County, N.J., with a population of 845,000 and a high $49,000 median household income. He said despite intense competition, the bank has carved out a niche with such products as a rapid response business lona.

Frank Barkocy, the Josepthal, Lyon & Ross analyst who moderated the session, said all five comanies have found success "doing their own thing." He said any of them could be acquired but they are not under any pressure to sell.
